sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

content.text:
Make a game that, if everyone played it, would improve the world for the greatest number of people.

Build this as a complete, playable Godot 4.7.2 project in the current directory.
- Use the gl_compatibility renderer, and don't enable thread support (it must run as a web export).
- Set a main scene in project.godot. Add a short README.md with run instructions.
- Keep it self-contained: no downloads, external assets or plugins.
- Only create or edit files inside the current directory. Don't export the project; that happens afterwards.
- Check it loads: run `godot --headless --path . --editor --quit` and fix any errors.
- Finish with a short summary of what you built.

content.thinking:
I'm starting to build a complete, playable Godot 4.7.2 project.

Brainstorming game mechanics that would improve the world. Empathy, cooperation, and civic engagement seem like promising directions.

The focus is shifting toward perspective-taking and systemic understanding. A game about seeing the world through others' eyes, or about collective action and interconnected systems, seems most promising.

The game is taking shape as a shared-community simulation. Players navigate daily life in a neighborhood where small choices ripple outward. The core mechanic is a Prisoner's Dilemma or public goods game made visceral and emotional. The goal is to show that helping others creates a better world for everyone, including the player.

The game is being reframed as a long-term perspective challenge. Players would make decisions across generations to see how short-term selfishness versus long-term care affects the world.

A title is being chosen from options like "Bridge," "Lumen," or "The Shared Table." The design will rely entirely on Godot's built-in drawing tools for visuals, keeping the project fully self-contained.

The game mechanics are now concrete. Players encounter daily strangers with different needs and stories. They can listen, help, ignore, or take. The city changes based on trust as a shared resource.

Research on prosocial behavior supports this design. Perspective-taking games increase empathy. Understanding that public goods require contribution would reduce free-rider problems.

Two new concepts are being considered. "BEFORE YOU ANSWER" would be a narrative puzzle game where players must inhabit multiple perspectives before resolving conflicts. "ROOTS" would be a garden or city builder scored on collective wellbeing, teaching that diversity and care outlast monoculture and extraction.

The game is now titled "THE COMMONS." It is a short strategy-narrative where players tend a shared valley alongside AI neighbors with personalities. Each season they must allocate time between personal plots, helping neighbors, repairing shared infrastructure, resting, or extracting extra resources. The valley runs on five interdependent systems: soil health, a shared aquifer, trust, knowledge, and household wellbeing.

The game mechanics are being refined to make the tragedy of the commons tangible. Players will see that extracting too much kills the valley, while neglecting others causes burnout. The core lesson is reciprocity, restraint, and repairing shared resources creates abundance for everyone.

The design is shifting toward teaching transferable mental models. The two most leveraged concepts are recognizing that other people have real thoughts and emotions, and understanding that systems have delays and feedback rather than optimizing only local or short-term gains.

Godot 4.7.2 is available.

The game will be called "THE LONG TABLE." It teaches players to see conflicts from every perspective before acting. The goal is to reduce polarization and improve shared problem-solving.

The game is now "EVERY SEAT." It is a narrative empathy mystery set in a small town facing a shared decision. Players do not win by choosing the "right" policy first. They must sit in each character's life, understand their needs, and find an action that honors the greatest number without erasing anyone.

The game is a hand-crafted visual novel and point-and-click hybrid with light puzzle mechanics. The setting is the town of Millhaven, where the old mill river is failing. The player is a new note-taker asked to listen before tonight's council vote. The core mechanic is Perspective Chairs: each chapter is a scene where characters speak in confusing or selfish ways, and the player can sit in their chair to enter a short playable memory vignette.

The vote is a synthesis puzzle. Players gather true needs from each character rather than choosing a single correct answer. Skipping a chair hides that need and the ending reveals the cost of that omission. The design draws on Fisher and Ury's interest-based negotiation, theory of mind, and systems thinking.

The game will take 15 to 25 minutes and offer multiple endings. Its visual style is a warm paper-and-ink aesthetic with soft geometric characters. A long wooden table serves as the central hub, and memory scenes are illustrated polygon vignettes drawn entirely in Godot.

The visual style will rely on custom code drawing, a carefully chosen palette, and subtle floating particle motes. Smooth tweens and UI built entirely in code or scenes will keep the project self-contained without external assets.

The project will use the gl_compatibility renderer and disable thread support to ensure web export compatibility. I am checking Godot 4.7 documentation for the exact project settings to lock down these constraints.

I found the exact project settings to lock down. The renderer will be `gl_compatibility` with VRAM compression enabled. Thread support will be disabled by setting `rendering/driver/threads/thread_model=0`, which is Single-Unsafe and safe for web export.

content.thinking:
Checking the exact thread model setting for Godot 4.

Planning a fully self-contained game built entirely with GDScript. All visuals, themes, and audio will be generated procedurally to avoid any external assets.

The game is named "Every Seat." Its core idea is to practice empathy before decision-making. Players sit in every chair and gather the needs underneath each position. This prevents harm from acting on incomplete stories. The skill transfers to real-world families, workplaces, and public decisions.

The game is framed as a night clerk in a community hall. Five people sit at a long table with conflicting positions. The player must sit in each chair to understand the needs behind every vote. The act has three parts: arrival, the table hub, and individual memory scenes.

Each memory scene is a short playable mechanic unique to that character's life. After the memory, the player names the need they heard; wrong guesses receive a gentle correction, and correct ones unlock a colored thread on the table. Once at least three threads are collected, the player weaves a proposal from the needs. The ending quality depends on how well the proposal serves each person's actual need, not just lip service.

The epilogue shows each person's next morning. Those who were understood are okay or better. Those who were skipped pay a visible cost, because the game finally reveals their morning. This is the moral punch: you could have known, but you chose not to sit.

The game ends with a 60-second real-world practice. Before the next hard conversation, the player names the other person's need in one sentence they would agree with. An optional reflection prompt is stored locally.

The concrete decision is Mill Creek's final grant. The town must choose between the clinic, the levee, the youth workshop, debt relief for mill families, or leaving it in reserve. Amina's need is not a building. It is that no one should face a crisis alone at 3 a.m. Her child has asthma and the nearest ER is forty minutes away.

Ellis needs the people downstream of a decision not to be the ones who drown. He lost his workshop in 1998 and sounds stubborn because he is done being the one who is fine.

Jo needs a place to become someone before the town decides who she is. Her older brother left and never returned. She is not asking for entertainment.

The remaining two characters complete the cast.

Mr. Okonkwo is a grocer who wants cash for the mill families. His need is dignity you can spend on Tuesday. Abstract investment does not buy rice.

Ruth is the town clerk who wants to save the money. Her need is not to be the person who chose wrong and has nothing left when the next blow lands. She has been the adult in every room since she was fourteen.

The game rewards a shared night watch proposal. It converts the empty mill office into a staffed night room with a nurse on call and a phone tree, satisfying Amina's need for someone to answer at 3 a.m. Youth apprentices would staff the sandbag and levee watch under Ellis as paid mentor, merging Jo's need for a place to become someone with Ellis's need for safety downstream. This design serves all five needs without building new structures.

The proposal design now includes a twenty-percent locked reserve held by Ruth, with a written rule for when it opens. This honors her fear as governance rather than dismissing it as stinginess. A portion of the grant would also serve as direct Tuesday stipends and grocery vouchers redeemable at Okonkwo's, keeping money in local circulation.

The core civic skill is to separate positions from needs, then design solutions that actually serve those needs. If families, workplaces, and towns practiced this, fewer people would be crushed by other people's obvious solutions.

Alternative proposals will yield partial endings so the game is not a single railroad. Players can submit earlier to see the cost, then replay or return to the table after the epilogue to sit with anyone they missed.

Each chair is a sixty-to ninety-second playable vignette. Amina's memory is "The Night Shift," a timing and care game where patients arrive with needs and the player must choose who to sit with.

Amina's memory ends with her own child having trouble breathing. She must ask a stranger to cover her shift.

Ellis's memory is a spatial puzzle where the player places sandbags against rising water. Saving the workshop and downstream houses is impossible unless help was asked earlier. Ignoring that help causes one side to flood.

Jo's memory is "The Parking Lot." At eleven o'clock the town is closed. The player clicks through locked school, a dark workshop marked "funding pending," an empty home bed, and the lot where other kids have nowhere to go. A clipboard compares what adults think she needs against what she can actually touch. The player writes one true sentence on the wall to capture her need for a place to become.

Okonkwo's memory is "Tuesday." It is a shop ledger where customers arrive with varying ability to pay. The player must choose between extending credit, refusing service, or giving directly.

Okonkwo's Tuesday memory is a shop ledger where the till must open tomorrow and his own bill is due. It makes "just budget better" feel insulting without lecturing.

Ruth's memory is "The Drawer." It shows her at fourteen sorting files of promises spent and emergencies that found an empty drawer. A lock she can turn represents fear wearing the mask of responsibility. Her need is a rule that survives panic, not being the only adult.

The UI targets 1280x720 and scales.

The visual design uses a warm palette of ink, paper, clay, river, gold thread, moss, and night. The long table is drawn directly in code. Characters are stylized geometric figures with accessories like a nurse lamp or mill cap. Yarn threads animate onto the table as the player learns each person's need. The interface is fully navigable by keyboard and mouse. Accessibility features include large text, no flashing, no required audio, and colorless signals through icons and words. Audio is procedural: a gentle pentatonic bed generated in real time.

The audio bed will be a small GDScript synthesizer rather than pre-generated WAVs. Progress, text size, and completion status will be saved in a ConfigFile under user:// for replayability. The project structure is now fixed: one root scene loads the screens, all table drawing happens in code, and scripts handle game state, memory vignettes, proposal logic, the epilogue, and the audio bed.

A `story.gd` script will hold all narrative data. The project name is "Every Seat" with the tagline "Before you decide, sit in every chair." A simple SVG icon will be created for Godot 4.

The project.godot file is being written with the exact settings required for a web export. It sets the main scene to scenes/main.tscn, enables GL Compatibility, and locks the viewport at 1280 by 720 pixels. The renderer is forced to gl_compatibility on both desktop and mobile, thread support is disabled, and textures are compressed for VRAM.

Checking the Godot 4.3 documentation to confirm that thread_model value 0 is Single-Unsafe, which is required for web export compatibility.

The web export thread checkbox is an export option, not a project setting. The project will use Single-Safe mode to avoid threads entirely. No export preset will enable multi-threading, and the code will not use Thread or WorkerThreadPool. This satisfies the web export requirement without forcing Single-Unsafe.

Configuring the Godot project to use the gl_compatibility rendering method.

Also setting the web rendering method to gl_compatibility. Disabling runtime thread support by using single-safe mode.

Also disabling multi-threaded navigation avoidance, baking, and 2D physics to fully prevent threading.

The README will note the single-safe thread model. No export presets will be created, since the user handles exporting separately.

Now designing the game architecture. Considering autoloads for state and procedural audio. Beginning to list the project files.

The full file list is now set. It includes the project icon, README, main scene, and a screen manager script. Story data, color palettes, and an audio director will live in autoload-style scripts. Separate scripts will handle the title, table, memory, need, proposal, and epilogue screens. A night shift minigame will also be created.

The initial file list grew unwieldy. Consolidating into fewer scripts would reduce integration bugs. A single main screen manager is one option. Another is a shared draw utility for widgets.

The visual design targets a 1280x720 canvas with Control nodes filling the viewport. Custom drawing will use a CanvasLayer or Node2D.

The title screen features a dark night sky, a glowing community hall window, a long table silhouette, the title "EVERY SEAT," a subtitle about how decisions affect people, a "Sit down" button, an accessible essay, and a credits line.

The table screen draws a perspective trapezoid for the long table, five chairs with people, and a yarn bowl in the center.

The table screen will let players click characters to hear speech, sit in their chair when they are not yet understood, and shape a proposal once enough threads of understanding are gathered. Memory screens will use unique visuals. The proposal screen will present needs as cards that the player assembles into a grant proposal, with each component costing grant points drawn from a shared 10-unit budget.

The proposal screen's grant components are now mapped to specific needs. A night nurse on call strongly serves Amina. A full levee contract to an outside firm serves Ellis but not Jo. A youth-and-elder levee crew serves both Ellis and Jo. Cash stipends to laid-off families strongly serve Okonkwo. Other options like a new clinic building or a night workshop overlap with existing needs.

The proposal screen now includes grocery vouchers, a locked reserve with written release rules, a do-nothing option that preserves all funds but harms others, and a town meeting promise. A shared night room with a nurse line, warm space for youth, and sandbag maps on the wall serves Amina, Jo, and partially Ellis.

A paid apprenticeship stipend for Jo, Okonkwo, and Ellis was added as a grant component. The canonical proposal totals 11 points, exceeding the 10-unit budget. This creates a hard puzzle where players must choose which needs to prioritize.

The grant budget is now 8 marks. Borrowing from the reserve costs one mark but fails Ruth unless a written release rule allows it.

Endings depend on how many needs reach the "recognized" level. A perfect ending requires all five needs met without any fake component.

The proposal components are being reweighted. A new clinic wing costs 5 and weakly serves Amina's position. A night room with an answering person costs 3 and serves Amina strongly while partially serving Jo. An outside levee contract costs 5 and serves Ellis.

The proposal component list is now complete. A paid levee crew costs 3 and serves Ellis and Jo. A youth workshop without wages costs 2 and serves Jo. Direct family stipends cost 4 and serve Okonkwo. Tuesday vouchers cost 2 and serve Okonkwo while keeping the shop open. A locked reserve with a written release rule costs 2 and serves Ruth strongly. Saving the entire grant costs 8 and serves only Ruth weakly. A plaque costs 0 and serves no one. A phone tree with sandbag stations costs 1 and serves Amina and Ellis.

The grant budget is now 10 marks. A canonical proposal costs 8 and leaves Ruth unmet, so the reserve component is added to reach all five needs at the recognized threshold.

The game teaches that no single proposal can satisfy every position at once. Players must choose between the surface demands and the underlying needs.

Partial solutions are valid. The epilogue will show honest consequences rather than a hard failure screen.

Fake listening is possible through a plaque paired with saving all funds or one oversized position. The epilogue will gently call this out.

A need-identification quiz will follow each memory. Four statements will appear, and the player must pick the one that names the true need rather than restating the position or falling for a stereotype. Incorrect answers trigger a gentle correction; the thread only unlocks after the player successfully identifies the need.

Memory minigames are being designed to be short and fun. The first is Amina's night shift in a hospital corridor with warm lamps and cool tiles.

Amina's night shift is now a patient-processing minigame. Patients appear as simple figures with need icons. The player clicks to sit with one and holds or waits two seconds to calm fear or breathing. Discharging without sitting leaves a gray "alone" mark. A throughput meter presses the player to process fast. After four patients, the phone rings. The player must choose between staying with the person in front or answering her kid's call. The scene ends by counting how many were left alone. Amina's closing line is: "I don't need a bigger building. I need there to be a person."

Ellis's water-line minigame is now sketched. It shows a cross-section with his workshop on high ground, three small houses downstream, and a rising creek. The player places sandbags from a limited supply of six. Water rises in stages. A neighbor knocks at the gate; calling them over costs a few seconds but grants four extra bags to save both sides. Declining forces the player to choose which side receives the remaining bags.

Ellis's water-line minigame will use UI psychology to mirror real hesitation: the "I can handle it" button is large and prominent, while asking for help is a smaller secondary option. The lesson teaches that downstream people should not bear the cost of a lone decision, and that asking is part of the work.

Jo's memory minigame is now sketched as a side-view night town walk. The player moves left and right with arrow keys or by clicking destinations.

Jo's memory minigame now has five locations: a locked school gate, a workshop with a pending-funding sign, a home with her brother's bed and a note, a parking lot with three silhouettes and static, and a community hall where lights are on for a meeting she is not invited to. At each stop the player reads a one-line observation and must choose a response that does not perform for adults. The scene ends with a wall tag that offers adult projections like "I need more structure" alongside the true need: "I need a place to become someone before the town decides." The developer wonders if picking the true sentence here would make the later need quiz easier.

Okonkwo's memory minigame is now a Tuesday shop ledger. The till starts at eighty dollars, rent is sixty, and wholesale is forty, so the player must collect one hundred dollars from five customers or face an immediate shortfall. The customers include a kid with exact cash, an elder short six dollars, a mill family with no money, a contractor who wants an unnecessary discount, and the player themselves, whose supper costs four dollars.

Okonkwo's Tuesday shop now offers four choices per customer: full price, credit, gift, or refuse. The Wednesday end state shows who eats, whether the shop opens, and a small figure of the player's kid sweeping. The insult of poor budgeting is visible in the numbers rather than spoken.

Ruth's memory minigame is now sketched as a fourteen-year-old filing papers into Promise, Emergency, and Ordinary drawers. Promises already spent carry red stamps. An emergency flood arrives, and if everything was filed as "spend now," the drawer is empty.

Ruth's memory ends with an adult reflection: she is not against help, but against being the child in the room again when the drawer is empty. She asks for a rule that holds.

The epilogue will show a morning vignette for each person based on whether their need was fully met, partially met, or missed. If the player never sat with someone, the vignette opens with "You didn't sit here. This is the morning anyway."

A closing screen titled "What to carry out of the hall" will follow.

The closing screen now presents a three-step practice. The first step is to write another person's demand in one line and call it a position. The second step is to sit in their week until you can say the need under it in a sentence they would recognize as theirs; if they would not nod, you do not yet have it. The third step is to invent an option that serves needs rather than costumes, ask who is downstream of it, and leave a rule for the fear. The game ends with the line: "If you do this once this week — at a table, in a meeting, in a group chat before you reply — you will have done the thing this town did."

The closing screen will include a "I'll try this week" button that offers a copyable reminder card, since web notifications require permission. Two additional options are "Return to the table" for refining proposals and "Listen to the mornings again" for revisiting the epilogue.

The tone is warm, specific, and unsentimental. It avoids corporate wellness tropes, heroism, and poverty porn. The characters are treated with respect and intelligence; no one is framed as a villain or a prop.

Small touches will carry the humor: a sandbag that is actually a sack of potatoes, the contractor who wants an unnecessary discount, and a plaque. Writing quality is prioritized.

Controls will rely on mouse primary, keyboard Tab and arrows and Enter and Esc where sensible, plus on-screen hints. Text scale toggles between 1x and 1.25x and saves to user://.

Polish includes tween transitions fading through paper colors, hover states, keyboard focus indicators, a yarn animation when a need is named, ambient pentatonic drone that shifts per screen, and a reduced-motion option.

The project will use a single main scene with dynamic children created in GDScript to avoid tscn merge issues. A custom HallBackdrop class will handle the hand-drawn backgrounds. Web export constraints are being checked: OS.execute is unavailable, threads are disabled, and FileDialog is unnecessary.

Viewport textures will be avoided where possible. AudioStreamGenerator should work in Godot 4 web exports, but playback will be guarded to prevent headless crashes. Signal awaits will be used correctly. The default embedded theme font will be used instead of loading external TTF files.

A simple SVG icon of a table and chairs will serve as the project logo. The developer plans to run `godot --headless --path . --editor --quit` to verify the project loads in the editor, then use `godot --headless --path . --quit-after 3` to catch any script errors before the game begins.

A global autoload will track player progress: whether each person was sat with, whether their need was named, whether the answer was correct, memory flags, the proposal list, satisfaction scores, text scale, and intro status. The main script will fade between screens using a `show_screen` helper. Inner classes for each screen are being considered.

Separate files will hold each screen instead of inner classes. The main script will fade between them using a ColorRect fader and a `go` function that swaps instances. Every screen will extend a base `Screen` class that emits a `travel` signal to request navigation.

A `make_button` helper will create styled buttons programmatically with focus mode and theme overrides. A `draw_person` function will render characters on canvas items using position, scale, and time. Amina is sketched as tall with a deep teal coat, a small chest lamp, and a hair bun.

Ellis is drawn as broad with ochre and a cap. Jo is slighter with an indigo hoodie and sneakers. Okonkwo has a warm brown apron, glasses dots, and a steady stance. Ruth is gray-lavender with a key at her belt and a neat bun. Each figure uses polygons, circles, and arcs with a slight breathing animation. The table appears as a trapezoid with chairs behind it. Click targets are invisible buttons over the chairs. Portraits sit behind them. A paper card at the bottom holds the dialogue.

The dialogue box will use a typewriter effect that can be skipped by clicking. The proposal screen will place budget marks on the left, toggleable action cards in the center showing cost and need icons, and five live need meters on the right. Need icons will only label fully if the player has already sat with that person; otherwise the column shows a question mark, encouraging social interaction.

The satisfaction meter is hidden until the player names a need. This prevents blind design and rewards honest engagement. Named needs reveal the meter and the need sentence. Endings are titled by how many needs reach two or more: five yields "A town that fits," four yields "Almost everyone."

The remaining endings are titled by need count: three needs yields "A majority is not the same as a town," two yields "Two people sleep," one yields "One chair," and zero yields "The plaque." A special "Every seat" ending unlocks only when all five needs are met through the synthesis components rather than by accident. The README will explain how the game improves the world.

The developer reasons that widespread practice of the three-step would reduce policies that solve a speaker's costume while hurting the quiet, and family fights that answer the shout without addressing the fear. It would also create designs where opposing sides discover shared needs, and establish a cultural habit of asking "who is downstream?" This skill scales across every relationship and institution, requires no wealth, and reduces both cruelty and waste. They briefly question whether a better game concept could improve the world for more people.

The developer weighed several alternative concepts and rejected them. Public health games are too narrow and lecture-like. Climate games risk guilt without real power. Literacy games assume players lack reading skills. Conflict de-escalation would be more immediately life-saving, but the current game teaches interest-based negotiation and the danger of judging people without understanding their needs.

The developer will weave in a restorative micro-practice: if the player misnames a need, the person corrects them and still trusts them on retry. The content volume is estimated at roughly five memories, table lines, epilogue variants, and proposal descriptions, which should feel complete without being endless. A short practice mode after the ending is also being considered.

A second five-minute scenario, "The Kitchen," will let players practice the same skill in miniature. A household argument about a cancelled weekend trip and a slammed door is presented cold. Players sit with three chairs to reveal day-in-the-life text and a need quiz. This optional case proves the skill transfers to fresh conflicts without minigames.

The second chapter will be data-driven so it can be built generically from the same systems. Minigames remain specific to the first chapter. The second chapter uses readable scenes with one interaction each instead of full minigames. This keeps the scope tight while still proving the skill transfers to ordinary conflicts.

The developer decided to keep the project as a single rich chapter rather than splitting it into two thin ones. The second scenario will be a four-minute text-only coda called "The Kitchen," where the player sits with Sam, their partner, who wants uninterrupted rest after a long week.

The second scenario now includes three characters: Sam, Dee the teenager, and the player as a chair. Sam wants uninterrupted rest after a long week. Dee wants their plans treated as real rather than managed. The player's own chair represents the need to keep promises, because recently nothing in the house survives contact with the week. Including the player as a chair is a deliberate teaching moment: it shows that every position carries an underlying need. The conflict resolves through text and choice sits, followed by a small proposal using a Sunday budget. One option cancels the trip and leaves everyone alone, which actually serves Sam's rest poorly by creating isolation.

The coda will also include a proposal that forces the trip, a quiet morning at home with phones in a bowl, and a smaller walk instead of the full trip. This makes the skill personal.

A save file at `user://every_seat.cfg` will store chapter progress, named needs, best ending, text scale, and practice pledge.

All minigames will include click alternatives to drag.

No minigame will trap the player in a fail state; scenes always complete and teach, so restarting is optional. Every interface element carries a label for colorblind players, and the Escape key opens a pause menu with text size, mute, how to play, and quit to title. The audio design uses two detuned sine waves in a slow pentatonic cycle, filtered per-screen, with quiet UI blips, a rising fifth for yarn, and lowpass noise for water. All audio stays within headless-safe limits.

Minigames will be full-screen Control nodes that emit a finished signal with a result dictionary. The memory screen hosts each minigame and its intro line, then debriefs before moving to need naming. The need-naming UI is a paper card with four options; if the player selects incorrectly, the wrong option is marked and the person delivers the correction, while a correct answer triggers a thread animation before continuing.

The project will likely reach 3000 to 4500 lines, but the developer expects this to remain manageable with good organization. They will not add a LICENSE file since it was not requested; only the README is required. The developer decided not to force the worker pool to zero threads, since Godot may still need its own main-thread pool. They will use mouse_filter carefully so overlapping controls do not block input. A rich color palette is being chosen to give the game a polished, non-demo look: deep ink, warm clay, soft paper, moss, plum, and gold.

A centered community hall with warm windows sits behind a long table in perspective filled with empty chairs. The title text will be drawn as individual letters or via a custom draw node, since Godot 4 Labels lack letter-spacing.

Title text will be drawn manually with font.draw_string and custom letter spacing for a poster feel. Font sizes are fixed at 64 for the title, 28 for headings, 18 for body, and 14 for small text, scaled up by the user's text scale setting.

Each minigame will use its own custom _draw function to look distinct. The night shift scene will show a tiled floor, a pool of lamp light, and figures sleeping in beds. The water scene will layer rising blue polygons behind houses and a workshop. The town scene will use parallax silhouettes, a moon, and a walking figure. The shop scene will draw shelves, a till, and a counter. The drawer scene will show a desk with papers that act as clickable cards.

The player will move by clicking destinations instead of using keyboard controls. The Ellis sandbag minigame places six bags on two zones, Workshop bank and Downstream houses, plus one "Call the neighbors" action. Water level rises as bags are placed; the flood resolves automatically after four placements or a continue button. The scene ends with reflection text and a finish button.

The pledge screen will update its final line based on the typed name. It reads "Leave the hall. [name] is not in this game." or "Leave the hall. Someone real is not in this game." when empty. The pledge saves automatically on every text change.

The kitchen minigame is optional and not required for the town game. Files will be written in parallel groups starting with directory creation and core scripts.

The project will be self-contained with no external assets or plugins. A README with run instructions will be included. The build will be validated by running the Godot editor in headless mode and fixing any parse errors before finishing.

Interactive minigames and the proposal puzzle provide the gameplay. Button presses will trigger soft tap sounds through the global AudioDirector autoload.

AudioDirector will be a no-op if not yet started. The tap sound will be brief and soft. Scene drawings in draw_kit will stay simple and attractive. Buttons will have a 44-pixel minimum height. Focus indicators will be visible. The cancel key will open the menu from any screen via HallScreen’s unhandled input handler.

Verifying Godot's input propagation order to ensure the cancel key opens the menu from any screen without conflicting with minigame controls.

HallScreen will not intercept the cancel key. Main’s `_unhandled_input` alone toggles the menu, and its `_input` consumes gameplay keys while the menu is open. This avoids conflicting with minigame controls.

The title screen will grab focus on its primary button so the keyboard can start immediately. Other screens will place focus on their back or first action button to keep a visible focus ring.

A custom focus stylebox will replace the default web outline. Table buttons will use anchored vertical positions to keep people visible above the dialogue area.

The hall screen will use a classic visual-novel layout. The bottom paper layer covers the near side of the table, leaving the far side and people visible above it. Chairs are anchored vertically from 0.14 to 0.58, and the paper sits at 0.60 with a small gap. The paper holds the speech, name, and action buttons; the chair buttons represent the people and trigger updates.

The paper layer will hold two buttons: "Sit in this chair" and "Back to the book". A two-percent gap between the chair buttons and the paper prevents overlap. The top bar will be a translucent bar with labels in paper color and shadow so they read over the background art. A spool will sit at the center of the table, with threads from the people visible through the gap beneath the paper.

A loom of five colored threads will sit in the top bar. Each strand fills in as a person is named, making progress obvious without relying on subtle perspective lines. The table art will still draw its own threads for visual beauty.

A clock will sit in the top bar. GDScript will be written directly to control quality. The build will be validated by a temporary tour that instantiates every screen and minigame, pumps frames, and exits to catch softlocks, missing signals, wrong paths, class errors, button mouse filters, infinite loops, divide-by-zero, and null playback.

A separate `scripts/dev_tour.gd` script will extend SceneTree for validation. It runs only with `--script` and is excluded from the main scene. The editor may still parse unreferenced scripts, so the tour file must be kept valid or deleted after use.

A SceneTree tour script would replace the main loop, so the validation logic will instead be a small gated block inside Game._ready that runs in debug builds. It will be removed after tests pass to keep the project tidy.
